paragraphs.heading: What meiosis is
paragraphs.text: Meiosis is a special kind of cell division that makes the sex cells, called gametes: sperm and eggs. It takes place in the germ cells of organisms that reproduce sexually. One cell divides twice in a row, in steps named meiosis I and meiosis II. The end result is four cells, and each holds just one copy of every chromosome, a state called haploid.

paragraphs.heading: Why halving matters
paragraphs.text: Halving the chromosomes is what lets sexual reproduction work. At fertilisation an egg and a sperm fuse into a zygote, a single cell holding two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent; a cell with two copies is called diploid. Human body cells, for example, carry 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Each egg or sperm carries one set of 23, so the zygote ends up with 46 again. Swinging back and forth between meiosis and fertilisation keeps the chromosome count steady from one generation to the next.

paragraphs.heading: Copying and pairing
paragraphs.text: Before the divisions begin, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical strands called sister chromatids, held together. The cell then enters a long stage called meiotic prophase. Here the matching chromosomes from mother and father, called homologs, line up in pairs. They swap pieces of DNA through recombination, a planned process of cutting and repairing the DNA. Some of these swaps leave crossovers, physical links between the pair called chiasmata.

paragraphs.heading: Two divisions
paragraphs.text: In the first division, a structure called the spindle apparatus pulls the members of each homolog pair into separate cells. The cells then divide a second time without copying their DNA again. This time the sister chromatids come apart, much as they do in mitosis, the ordinary division that turns one cell into two identical ones. That leaves four haploid cells in all.

paragraphs.heading: A source of variety
paragraphs.text: Because of recombination, a single chromatid can carry a fresh mix of the mother's and the father's genetic information. On top of that, each gamete gets its own blend of maternal, paternal and mixed chromatids. That is why offspring differ genetically from both parents. This variety feeds the differences in traits that natural selection works on.

paragraphs.heading: Where it happens
paragraphs.text: Meiosis is found in every sexually reproducing organism, single-celled or many-celled, including animals, plants and fungi. In some cases all four products become gametes, spores or pollen. In female animals, though, three of the four are usually cast off as small polar bodies, and only one becomes an egg. Bacteria and archaea do not use meiosis at all.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Mistakes in meiosis can produce aneuploidy, meaning an abnormal number of chromosomes. These errors are the biggest known reason for miscarriage, and they are the most frequent genetic source of developmental disabilities.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: Oscar Hertwig, a German biologist, first described meiosis in 1876 while studying sea urchin eggs. In 1883 Edouard Van Beneden described it again, this time at the level of chromosomes, in the eggs of the Ascaris roundworm. In 1890 August Weismann explained why it matters: to keep the chromosome number steady, one diploid cell must divide twice to give four haploid cells. In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan spotted crossovers in fruit flies, which helped show that traits are carried on chromosomes.
